rationale: Yway (open XLM-R encoder with Laya's decision head, Burmese) transfers to unseen question wordings only where training wordings were broad (unseen-wording test: answerable 0.92, relevance 0.86, topic-is-X 0.89) but 'has a number' falls from 0.995 on training wordings to 0.579, the held-out register task stays at chance (0.51-0.53), and zero-shot Laya multilingual (mmBERT) scores 0.120 accuracy with ECE 0.808 on 569 Burmese topic texts against 0.863 after fine-tuning (Sec. 4.2, Table 2; Sec. 5.3-5.4, Fig. 7).

With one temperature per question type fitted on validation, held-out ECE is 0.006-0.035 on most tasks but 0.114 on the 12-way topic choice; the answer checker reaches ECE 0.013 only after training on 22,000 real judged Gemma 3 12B answers, having scored judge-correct and judge-wrong answers 0.89 vs 0.91 when trained on rule-made negatives (Sec. 4.3, 5.1-5.2, Fig. 4).

Used as a filter on 2,000 real Gemma 3 12B answers, the checker at threshold 0.5 catches 81% of wrong answers while keeping 68% of correct ones, raising shown-answer quality from 0.44 to 0.68 (0.81 at 0.7 with 14% shown), but it works only after training on real judged errors and judges answers with one changed number correctly only 45% of the time; the proposed show/retrieve/'I don't know' bands (0.6/0.3) were not evaluated (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 5).

Called once per relation with only three English labels and no evidence, Jev chose the 'maybe' option for 1.0% (163/15,925) and 0.8% (196/24,800) of flagged Wikidata relations, and identical or symmetric inputs received different verdicts in 7/46 and 4/127 duplicate-triple groups and 18/1,836 and 22/445 reciprocal diplomatic-relation pairs; verdicts were never checked against human judgement (Sec. 4.1, 5.1, 5.5; Tables 3, 8).

With no evidence, jev-1.13.0 Choice puts 0.83-0.93 on 'heads' under all six label sets, a pull carried by the option word (+0.354 [0.347, 0.361]) rather than key name (+0.027) or list position (-0.015) when options have descriptions; one 55%-reliable witness cuts it to +0.063, the Choice step survives three wordings (45%->55% jump 0.59-0.89), and Laya instead shows key (+0.28) and first-position (+0.15) bias (Sec. 4.1-4.2; Tables 1, 2, 6).

On exact-target cases, Choice behaves as a step (a 45%->55% stated base rate raises it by 0.83-0.98 against a correct 0.10; holdout Brier 0.0665, temperature-scaled still 55x worse than Noul on base rates) while Noul stays within 0.015-0.027 of stated rates (normalized Noul Brier 0.0034 [0.003, 0.004]); on 650 human-vote items normalized Noul beats Choice (ChaosNLI Brier 0.096 vs 0.203) but neither beats a uniform guess on the most contested bin (0.135/0.321 vs 0.058), and the open Laya, Qwen3-0.6B PSR-FT and eve-rlcd models ignore stated rates (jump <=0.06) (Sec. 4.2-4.4, 5; Tables 3-6).

As a stand-in for crowd vote distributions, Choice reports 0.80 where the ChaosNLI majority holds 45% and 0.88 on DICES-350 safety items split 55/45 and is worse than a uniform guess on every DICES measure (Brier 0.092 vs 0.071); normalized Noul is closer (ChaosNLI Brier 0.096 vs uniform 0.240) but loses to uniform on DICES KL (0.226 vs 0.158) and on contested items, and one fitted temperature equalizes the two only on average while under-confident on clear items (Sec. 4.4; Table 5; App. E, Table 8).

Reversing the option order changed the released Noma model's prediction on 9.7% [6.2, 14.8] of 186 sealed-set choice items and a seeded random reordering on 7.0% [4.1, 11.6], with accuracy unchanged (83.9% vs 84.9%) and changes concentrated on low-confidence items (mean 0.52 vs 0.90); at most 2 of 36 confident easy/original-tier items changed (Sec. 7.2; Table A5).

After per-type temperature scaling, sealed-set confidence 84.7% matches accuracy 82.6% (ECE 0.043, n=386) and ECE is 0.060/0.070 on unseen Banking77/CLINC150 label sets, but on 56 held-out multi-step items confidence is 70.8% against 48.2% accuracy (ECE 0.282); the abstain head separates the 15 unsupported items only when supervised (AUROC 0.82 [0.70, 0.93] vs 0.46 [0.32, 0.60]) and ranks CLINC150 out-of-scope queries (AUROC 0.97) while staying below 0.5, so it needs a tuned threshold (Sec. 5.2, 6.2; Tables 1, 3).

Answering only the most confident half of the sealed set gives 96.9% accuracy (89.6% at 80% coverage), but on held-out multi-step items the model is right about a third of the time between 0.5 and 0.9 stated confidence, so a threshold below 0.9 does not route them away, and head disagreement detects errors worse than maximum probability (AUROC 0.59 vs 0.81 for the released model) (Sec. 5.2; Fig. 5; Table A4).

In two Human-Gated live calls (requested jev-latest, resolved jev-1.13.0) the four-label decisions (SUFFICIENT 0.86 with confidence 0.82; INSUFFICIENT 1.00) were persisted with raw-response hashes and both decision paths were RECONSTRUCTED, but only inside a consumer-built deterministic shell (prechecks, contract validation, evidence persistence; 124/124 offline tests, 0 fail-open across 20 injected failure cases), and the output carried no reasons; n=2, one call each (README 'J6 Bounded Live Observations'; J6 Closeout Sec. 5-7; J4_Implementation).

As a typed per-turn supervisor mapping eight Noul/Choice/Score judgments to fixed controls for a claude-sonnet-5 coding agent on held-out SWE-bench Verified tasks, active Jev resolved 62.3% vs 55.1% unsupervised (+7.2 pp, 95% CI -4.3 to +18.8, n=69, p=.332), while a no-message shadow arm was +8.5 pp over none (CI 0.0 to +16.9, n=71, post hoc) and active only +1.6 pp over shadow (CI -6.5 to +9.7, n=62), so no intervention effect was resolved (Sec. 5.1-5.2; Table 2).

Over 14,642 moves in its own gridworld games, jev-1.13.0 gave chosen moves a mean probability of 0.72 while 51% were optimal (ECE 0.21; Brier 0.283 vs 0.250 for a constant), though moves at >=0.9 were optimal 74% of the time vs 42% below and its exam ECE was 0.06; the chat model Qwen3.5-4B read through option-number probabilities had ECE 0.06 and was the only model beating a constant (Brier 0.232 vs 0.249), while open Laya (ECE 0.13) and GLiClass (0.33) were also worse than a constant (Sec. 5.7; Fig. 6; App. B, H7).

Trained on Norwegian and Austrian register texts, the open SignRule-Decide 4B model agreed with the AI-consensus reference on 99.3% of Austrian coalition questions and 94.6% of rule types (n=400), but on 300 Danish texts from a register never seen in training it reached 92.5% on coalitions and 62.4% on rule type, misreading Danish 'direktionen' as a collective body (Sec. 7; Tables 3, 5).

With temperatures per question type fitted on validation, register-labelled test ECE was 0.002/0.007 (H2 met) and dangerous yes/no errors were 12 of 2,178 (0.6%) on the Austrian reference set, but 10 of the 12 were given with confidence >=0.9, the explicit abstention left 99.9% of Austrian questions answered, and minimum signers derived from the model's own coalition answers reached only 77.7% (H16 not met) (Sec. 5, 7; Table 3; App. A).

Learn-then-Test abstention thresholds fitted on Norwegian and Austrian validation held observed risk to 1.3% at 99.9% coverage against a 2% target on Austria (H22 met), but on the unseen Danish register they certified answering everything and the observed risk was 14.3% against a 5% target (H18 not met), with errors at high confidence (Sec. 7; Fig. 1; App. A, Table 7).
